Cutting a magnet never produces an isolated pole. The chapter states this directly: if a magnet is broken into two or more pieces then each piece behaves like an independent magnet with a somewhat weaker magnetic field, and isolated magnetic monopoles do not exist. What does change is the magnetic dipole moment, and it changes for a different reason in each of the two cuts.

Write the original magnet as pole strength \(q_{m}\) at each end and magnetic length \(2l\), so that \(m = q_{m} \cdot 2l\).

**Cut transverse to the length** (a cut across the bar, perpendicular to its axis): each half keeps the whole pole face, so its pole strength is still \(q_{m}\), while its magnetic length is halved to \(l\). A new S pole and a new N pole appear on the two faces of the cut, so each piece is a complete magnet with
\(m' = q_{m}\cdot l = \dfrac{m}{2}\)

**Cut along the length** (a cut parallel to the axis): each half keeps the full magnetic length \(2l\), but its pole face has half the original area, so its pole strength halves to \(q_{m}/2\). Each piece is again a complete magnet, with
\(m' = \dfrac{q_{m}}{2}\cdot 2l = \dfrac{m}{2}\)

So in both cases we are left with two shorter or thinner bar magnets, each of half the original magnetic moment, and each still carrying an N pole and an S pole. Repeating the cut only gives weaker dipoles; it never gives a monopole.

Gauss' law of magnetism as the chapter states it is
\(\Phi_{B} = \displaystyle\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{S} = 0\)
and the right-hand side is zero only because no closed surface can enclose a net pole strength — even a thin slice of a bar magnet carries both an N and an S pole, so whatever flux enters the surface leaves it again.

If a monopole of pole strength \(p\) could be enclosed, that cancellation would fail and the right-hand side would be proportional to \(p\). The constant of proportionality follows from the electrostatic analogue of Table 12.1. In electrostatics the chapter writes
\(\Phi_{E} = \displaystyle\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S} = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_{0}}\)
and the table pairs the electrostatic constant \(\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\) with the magnetic constant \(\dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\). Replacing \(\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon_{0}}\) by \(\mu_{0}\) and the charge \(q\) by the pole strength \(p\) gives

\(\Phi_{B} = \displaystyle\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{S} = \mu_{0}\,p\)

This is the form Gauss' law of magnetism would take in a world with monopoles. It reduces to the printed \(\Phi_{B} = 0\) whenever the net pole strength enclosed is zero — which, as the chapter emphasises, is every case we actually meet.

**Statement.** The net magnetic flux through any closed (Gaussian) surface is zero:
\(\Phi_{B} = \displaystyle\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{S} = 0\)

**Why it takes this form.** The chapter argues it from the shapes of the field lines in Fig. 12.4, using two different closed surfaces drawn on the same magnet.

Surface (i) is drawn in the region outside the magnet and encloses no pole. Counting the lines of force entering it and the lines leaving it gives the same number, so the two contributions cancel and the flux through it is zero.

Surface (ii) is drawn so that it encloses the north pole. One might expect a net outward flux, as would happen for a charge. It does not happen, because a magnetic pole cannot be isolated: even a thin slice of a bar magnet has an N pole and an S pole, so the closed surface that catches the N pole necessarily catches an S pole too, and the flux again cancels. The same holds for the current-carrying solenoid of Fig. 12.4(b).

**Contrast with electrostatics.** For the electric dipole of Fig. 12.4(c) the lines begin on the positive charge and end on the negative one without closing, so a closed surface round the positive charge alone has a genuine net outward flux, \(\Phi_{E} = \displaystyle\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S} = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_{0}}\). It is precisely this option that magnetism does not offer.

**What it tells us.** Because the law holds for every closed surface however drawn, magnetic lines of force can have no beginning and no end — they must form closed loops. An isolated electric charge exists but an isolated magnetic pole does not; in magnetism only dipoles (and higher arrangements such as quadrupoles) occur.

[Textbook misprint in the theory this question examines: section 12.5 defines the geographic meridian as "a plane perpendicular to the surface of the Earth (vertical plane) perpendicular to geographic axis". "Perpendicular to" should read "passing through". A plane perpendicular to the geographic axis is the equatorial plane, which is not vertical and is not a meridian at all, so the printed definition is self-contradictory. Three parts of the book itself give the correct form: the magnetic meridian is defined one line below as a vertical plane "passing through the magnetic axis"; Fig. 12.6 draws the geographic meridian as a vertical plane containing the geographic North-South line; and this chapter's own Exercise Q.1 (ii) offers "passing through the geographic axis" as the geographic-meridian alternative. Declination, defined as the angle between the two meridians, would also be meaningless if one of them were the equatorial plane. The answer above uses the corrected definition.]

**Geographic meridian.** At any place on the Earth the geographic meridian is the vertical plane — a plane perpendicular to the Earth's surface there — that contains the geographic axis, that is the plane containing the true (geographic) North-South line through the place. It is the reference plane against which the magnetic meridian, the vertical plane through the magnetic axis, is compared; the angle between the two is the magnetic declination \(\alpha\), as drawn in Fig. 12.6.

**Variation of declination with latitude.** Declination measures how far the magnetic meridian at a place has swung away from the geographic one, so it depends on where that place stands relative to the Earth's magnetic axis, which is tilted with respect to the axis of rotation. Near the magnetic equator the two meridians are nearly parallel and the declination is small; as one moves to higher latitudes, towards a magnetic pole, the magnetic meridian swings further from the geographic meridian and the declination grows, becoming very large close to a magnetic pole, where the horizontal component vanishes and the magnetic meridian is no longer well defined at all.

**Where it is minimum.** The declination is minimum — in fact exactly zero — at places where the magnetic meridian coincides with the geographic meridian, so that a compass needle points to true North. These places lie broadly at low latitudes, and the chapter's own Indian data show one such line passing through the country: the declination is \(0^{\circ}58'\) **west** at Mumbai and \(0^{\circ}41'\) **east** at Delhi, so it changes sign, and therefore passes through zero, somewhere between the two.

[Note: the chapter states that the declination is small in India and gives the two values above, but it does not itself set out the latitude dependence; the general behaviour described here follows from the definition of declination together with the tilt of the magnetic axis shown in Fig. 12.5.]

**Definition.** The angle of dip (or magnetic inclination) \(\phi\) at a place is the angle made by the direction of the resultant magnetic field of the Earth with the horizontal at that place (Fig. 12.7). Resolving that field into a horizontal component \(B_{H}\) and a vertical component \(B_{V}\),
\(B_{H} = B\cos\phi\), \(B_{V} = B\sin\phi\)
so that
\(\tan\phi = \dfrac{B_{V}}{B_{H}}\)     ... (12.10)
It is the angle a dip needle, free to rotate in a vertical plane in the magnetic meridian, settles at.

**Behaviour from the magnetic equator to the magnetic pole.** The chapter's special cases fix the two ends of the range.

At the magnetic equator the field is horizontal, along South to North: \(B = B_{H}\), \(B_{V} = 0\), so \(\tan\phi = 0\) and \(\phi = 0^{\circ}\).

At a magnetic pole the field is entirely vertical: \(B = B_{V}\), \(B_{H} = 0\), so \(\tan\phi\) is undefined and \(\phi = 90^{\circ}\) — pointing downward at the magnetic north pole and upward at the magnetic south pole.

So as we move from the magnetic equator towards a magnetic pole, \(B_{V}\) grows and \(B_{H}\) falls, the ratio \(B_{V}/B_{H}\) increases steadily, and the angle of dip increases continuously from \(0^{\circ}\) at the magnetic equator to \(90^{\circ}\) at the magnetic pole. The dip needle, horizontal at the equator, tilts more and more until it stands vertical at the pole.

**Data.** Pole strength of the isolated pole \(q_{m} = 100\,\text{A m}\); distance from the centre of the bar magnet \(r = 20\,\text{cm} = 0.2\,\text{m}\); pole strength of the bar magnet \(q_{M} = 200\,\text{A m}\); its magnetic length \(2l = 5\,\text{cm} = 0.05\,\text{m}\); the pole lies on the axis of the bar magnet.

**Step 1 — magnetic moment of the bar magnet.**
\(M = q_{M}\times 2l = 200 \times 0.05 = 10\,\text{A m}^{2}\)

**Step 2 — field of the bar magnet at the location of the pole.** The point is on the axis and \(r \gg 2l\), so the short-dipole axial field of Eq. (12.3) applies:
\(B_{a} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{2M}{r^{3}} = \dfrac{10^{-7}\times 2 \times 10}{(0.2)^{3}} = \dfrac{2\times 10^{-6}}{8\times 10^{-3}}\)
\(B_{a} = 2.5\times 10^{-4}\,\text{T}\)

**Step 3 — force on the pole.** From the magnetic entry of Table 12.1, \(\vec{F} = q_{m}\vec{B}\):
\(F = q_{m}B_{a} = 100 \times 2.5\times 10^{-4}\)

\(F = 2.5\times 10^{-2}\,\text{N}\)

The force acts along the axis of the bar magnet, and is one of attraction or repulsion according to which pole of the bar magnet faces the given pole. This agrees with the answer printed in the book.

[Note: the short-dipole formula is an approximation here, since \(2l\) is not utterly negligible against \(r\). Using the exact two-pole expression \(F = q_{m}\dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}q_{M}\left[\dfrac{1}{(r-l)^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{(r+l)^{2}}\right]\) gives \(2.58\times 10^{-2}\,\text{N}\), about 3% higher. The printed answer is the short-dipole value.]

**Idea.** A dip needle reads the true dip only when it swings in the magnetic meridian. Turned into any other vertical plane it reads an **apparent** dip, because the plane picks up only the component of the horizontal field that lies in it, while the vertical field is unchanged.

**Set-up.** Let \(\phi\) be the true dip and let the plane of swing make an angle \(\theta\) with the magnetic meridian. The vertical component in that plane is still \(B_{V}\); the horizontal component resolved into the plane is \(B_{H}\cos\theta\). Hence the apparent dip \(\phi'\) obeys
\(\tan\phi' = \dfrac{B_{V}}{B_{H}\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\tan\phi}{\cos\theta}\)
using Eq. (12.10), \(\tan\phi = B_{V}/B_{H}\). Rearranging,
\(\tan\phi = \tan\phi' \cos\theta\)

**Substituting.** Here the magnet settles at \(\phi' = 45^{\circ}\) in a plane at \(\theta = 30^{\circ}\) to the magnetic meridian:
\(\tan\phi = \tan 45^{\circ} \times \cos 30^{\circ} = 1 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 0.866\)

\(\therefore \phi = \tan^{-1}(0.866) \approx 40^{\circ}54'\)

The true dip is smaller than the apparent dip, as it must be, since \(\cos\theta < 1\) for any plane away from the magnetic meridian. This agrees with the answer printed in the book.

**Geometry.** Call the magnets 1 and 2, each of moment \(m = 1.0\,\text{A m}^{2}\), with centres \(2\,\text{m}\) apart, so the mid-point O of the line joining the centres is \(r = 1\,\text{m}\) from each. The axes are perpendicular to each other, and the line joining the centres is drawn along the axis of one magnet. Therefore, taking magnet 1 to be the one whose axis lies along that line:

- O lies on the **axis** of magnet 1;
- O lies on the **equator** of magnet 2, because magnet 2's axis is perpendicular to the joining line.

**Field due to magnet 1 (axial).** By Eq. (12.3),
\(B_{1} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{r^{3}} = \dfrac{10^{-7}\times 2 \times 1.0}{1^{3}} = 2\times 10^{-7}\,\text{T}\)
directed along \(\vec{m}_{1}\), i.e. along the joining line.

**Field due to magnet 2 (equatorial).** By Eq. (12.4),
\(B_{2} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{r^{3}} = \dfrac{10^{-7}\times 1.0}{1^{3}} = 1\times 10^{-7}\,\text{T}\)
directed opposite to \(\vec{m}_{2}\), i.e. perpendicular to the joining line.

**Resultant.** The two contributions are mutually perpendicular, so they add in quadrature:
\(B = \sqrt{B_{1}^{2} + B_{2}^{2}} = \sqrt{(2\times 10^{-7})^{2} + (1\times 10^{-7})^{2}}\)
\(B = 10^{-7}\sqrt{4 + 1}\)

\(B = \sqrt{5}\times 10^{-7}\,\text{T} \approx 2.24\times 10^{-7}\,\text{T}\)

Its direction makes an angle \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{B_{2}}{B_{1}}\right) = \tan^{-1}(0.5) \approx 26^{\circ}34'\) with the joining line. This agrees with the answer printed in the book.

The answer to both parts of this question is a drawing; what follows is the description the drawing must satisfy.

**Part 1 — the field in the gap of one such magnet.** Draw a small circular N pole at the centre, and round it, separated by an air gap, an annular (ring-shaped) S pole. In the gap the lines of force must obey the rules of section 12.2: they leave the north pole, enter the south pole, never intersect, and close on themselves through the body of the magnet.

Because the central pole is a point of symmetry and the outer pole is a ring concentric with it, the lines in the gap are **straight radial lines** running outward from the central N pole in every direction to the surrounding S ring — like the spokes of a wheel, evenly spaced, arrowheads pointing outward. Their density, and hence the field, is greatest close to the central pole and falls off outward, since the same lines spread over an ever larger circumference. Inside the material of the magnet the same lines return from the S ring to the N centre, closing each loop.

**Part 2 — between the south poles of two such magnets.** Place two of these magnets side by side, so that the two outer S rings face each other. Each S ring is a sink of lines of force, so in the region between them the lines from the two magnets arrive head-on, in opposite directions. Draw the lines curving away from the line joining the two centres and bending back into their own S rings, so that no line from one magnet ever enters the other and no two lines cross. Midway between the two magnets the two contributions are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so they cancel: mark that point as a **neutral point**, where the resultant magnetic field is zero and no line of force passes. The pattern is the mirror image, about the mid-plane, of the like-pole repulsion picture — the lines are pushed apart sideways in the middle region.

The answer to this question is a drawing; what follows is the description the drawing must satisfy.

**Arrangement.** Draw the two bar magnets end to end on a straight line, with their north poles facing each other across a gap: reading left to right, S-N ... N-S.

**The lines of force.** Each magnet on its own has lines that leave its N pole, sweep round outside and enter its S pole, closing through the magnet itself. Draw these for each magnet, and then, in the region between the two facing north poles, remember that no two lines may intersect and that both sets are directed **outward** from their own N pole. The two families therefore meet head-on, and are pushed sideways: the lines emerging from the left magnet's N pole curve sharply up and down, away from the axis, and return to that magnet's own S pole; the lines from the right magnet's N pole do the same in mirror image. No line crosses from one magnet into the other, and the region directly between the poles is left almost empty of lines — the characteristic picture of like poles repelling.

**The neutral point.** On the axis, between the two north poles, the field of the left magnet points to the right and that of the right magnet points to the left. Somewhere between them the two are equal in magnitude and cancel, and the resultant field is zero. Mark that point with a cross or a dot labelled **N.P.** For two identical magnets, symmetry places it exactly at the **mid-point of the line joining the two north poles**; if the magnets are of unequal strength it lies nearer the weaker one. There is only one such point on the axis, and it is where the two opposing families of lines separate — no line of force passes through it.

[Note: the neutral point here is produced by the two magnets alone. If the Earth's horizontal field \(B_{H}\) is also taken into account, as it is in the chapter's worked Example 12.3, its position shifts, since the resultant must then cancel three contributions rather than two.]
